minor: 'a bust of Lenin' in Barentsburg is true but has no entry in the sources list; add one or cut it.
'Norway's motto is High North, low tension' is better called a policy slogan or the title of its High North strategy; the source is a government strategy, not a motto.

'before aircraft had even flown to the Pole': the Norge flight of May 1926 is the usual first, but Byrd's disputed claim from earlier that month exists. Say 'before any airship or aircraft had crossed the Pole' to be safe.
'Slightly more than the whole of Croatia' is about 8% more (61,022 vs 56,594 km²). 'A little larger than Croatia' is a closer match.

Article 3 gives equal 'access and entry' and equal rights to maritime, industrial, mining and commercial operations. 'Live' is not literally in the article; it follows from the entry rights plus Norway's own policy. The cold-open line 'A 1920 treaty lets citizens of over 40 countries live here' compresses this.
The 2019 ruling is described as a licence 'not only an EU one'. The court held that the vessel needed a Norwegian licence under Norwegian law. The EU licence detail is background, not the holding.

shots.vo: So why does Svalbard have no visa, and why can't Norway change it?
The answer starts in 1596, with a Dutch ship.

shots.vo: Svalbard is a cluster of Arctic islands lying between 74 and 81 degrees north, far above mainland Norway.
Its main town, Longyearbyen, is about 960 kilometres north of Tromsø, one of the mainland cities with direct flights there.
From Longyearbyen, the North Pole is only about 1,310 kilometres further north.
The islands cover about 61,000 square kilometres, slightly more than the whole of Croatia.

shots.vo: More than half of that land lies under glaciers, and about two thirds of it is protected nature.
Most people live along one fjord, Isfjorden, on Spitsbergen, the biggest island.
Longyearbyen and the research village of Ny-Ålesund, the Norwegian settlements, are home to about 2,500 people.
About 36 kilometres west-southwest, in a straight line, lies Barentsburg, a Russian coal town of a few hundred people.
Its streets still keep a bust of Lenin, and the mine belongs to Arktikugol, a Russian state company.

shots.vo: Further north stands a second Soviet town, Pyramiden, closed in 1998 and now visited mainly by tourists.
In the Norwegian settlements, roughly one resident in three is a foreign citizen.

shots.vo: The largest foreign groups come from Thailand, Sweden and the Philippines, Statistics Norway reports.
What lets them come is one article: Article 3 of the treaty signed in Paris in 1920.
It gives citizens of every country that joined equal rights to enter, live, work, mine and trade here.

shots.vo: So Norway asks newcomers for neither a visa nor a work permit, and it applies that to every nationality.

map.label: No visa · no work permit · any nationality

shots.vo: The catch is the journey: scheduled flights come through mainland Norway, which belongs to Europe's Schengen area.
So travellers who need a Schengen visa usually need one just to pass through Oslo or Tromsø, the Governor's office says.
And the Governor can refuse or remove people who cannot support themselves, under Norway's Svalbard rules.

So why would a country accept an open door like this on its own land?

shots.vo: Because until 1920, no country governed Svalbard at all.

shots.vo: In June 1596, Dutch navigator Willem Barentsz sighted these islands while hunting for a northern sea route to Asia.
He named them Spitsbergen, Dutch for pointed mountains, after the jagged peaks along the west coast.
Whalers followed, and by 1619 the Dutch had built a whaling station called Smeerenburg in the far northwest.
England, the Netherlands and Denmark-Norway each claimed the islands, and their whalers clashed over the best bays.
When the whales grew scarce, the claims went quiet, and no state took charge of the islands.
Then came coal: in 1906, the American businessman John Munro Longyear founded the mining town that bears his name.
British, Swedish, Russian and Norwegian companies staked claims across the same valleys, with no court to settle disputes.
Norway, Sweden and Russia met in Kristiania, today's Oslo, in 1910, 1912 and 1914; each time the talks failed, and the islands stayed on the map as no-one's land.
Then the First World War broke out, and the question moved to the peace conference in Paris.
On 9 February 1920, nine signatory powers signed the Spitsbergen Treaty, giving Norway full and absolute sovereignty.

document.title: Treaty concerning the Archipelago of Spitsbergen, Paris, 9 February 1920, Article 1
document.highlight: The High Contracting Parties undertake to recognise, subject to the stipulations of the present Treaty, the full and absolute sovereignty of Norway over the Archipelago of Spitsbergen.

shots.vo: That drew the first line: every island from Bear Island to the far north became Norwegian territory.
But the price came in the same text: Article 9 bans any naval base or fortification on the islands.

quote.text: Norway undertakes not to create nor to allow the establishment of any naval base... and not to construct any fortification in the said territories, which may never be used for warlike purposes.
quote.source: Treaty concerning the Archipelago of Spitsbergen, 9 February 1920

shots.vo: Article 8 says taxes raised on Svalbard may only be spent on Svalbard; Norway's own tax rules keep rates low.
One great power was missing from Paris: Soviet Russia, then not recognised by the Western allies.
In 1924 Moscow accepted Norway's rule, and on 14 August 1925 Norway formally took over the islands.
In 1932, Arktikugol, a Soviet state trust, bought the Barentsburg mine from its Dutch owners.
In the Second World War, the settlements were evacuated in 1941, and German warships attacked them in 1943.

shots.vo: After 1945, Norwegian and Soviet miners came back, and the emptied settlements were rebuilt on the same sites.
In November 1944, Soviet foreign minister Vyacheslav Molotov asked Norway for joint defence of the islands and for Bear Island.

shots.vo: Bear Island lies about 420 kilometres off Norway's North Cape, beside the sea lane from Russia's northern ports.
In February 1947, Norway's parliament declined the Soviet request.

shots.vo: So the 1920 line stayed exactly where it was drawn, from Bear Island in the south to the far north.
In 1977, Norway drew a second line, at sea: a fisheries protection zone reaching 200 nautical miles from the coast.
The Fisheries Directorate puts that zone at about 804,000 square kilometres, some thirteen times the land.
Norway lets other countries' fleets fish there, but only under Norwegian quotas and inspections.

shots.vo: So who owns the fish and the seabed inside that line? A century on, the treaty states still disagree.

shots.vo: Norway's reading is that the treaty's equal rights cover the islands and their 12-nautical-mile territorial waters, nothing more.

map.label: Treaty area, Norway says: land + 12 nm

shots.vo: Beyond that, Norway says, the zone and seabed are its own under the UN Law of the Sea, the 1982 ocean treaty.
Russia does not recognise the zone, and Iceland, Spain and the EU have challenged how Norway applies its rules there.
Their strongest argument: the zone exists only because Svalbard exists, so the treaty's equal rights should follow it out to sea.
The question reached Norway's Supreme Court through a seabed animal: the snow crab.

shots.vo: On a plateau above Longyearbyen, more than 100 antennas form one of the world's largest satellite ground stations.
So close to the Pole, it can reach satellites in polar orbit on every single pass around the Earth.
Their data runs down to the mainland through two subsea fibre cables completed in 2004.
In January 2022, one of those two cables was damaged on the seabed; investigators did not publicly name a cause.
In 2017, Russia's foreign ministry protested when a NATO parliamentary meeting was held in Longyearbyen.
In February 2020, at the treaty's centenary, foreign minister Sergei Lavrov wrote to Norway and set out Russia's case.
Russia's foreign ministry argues that Norway's sovereignty is granted only subject to the treaty's equal rights (Article 1), and that Norwegian rules on Russian activity empty those rights out.
Norway replied that no bilateral talks were needed, because its rules on Svalbard apply equally to everyone.

shots.vo: Norway's case: it holds sovereignty, allows no naval base, and applies one set of rules to Norwegians and foreigners alike.
One building shows the shared spirit best: the Global Seed Vault, cut into a mountain near the airport, opened in 2008.
Countries from around the world now store more than 1.2 million seed samples inside, as a backup for farming.

So what happens to this map if the ice, the fish or the politics change?

shots.vo: Sea ice around the islands has shrunk, opening water that used to stay frozen for much of the year.
So far, every line on this map has held: 1920 on land, 1977 at sea, 2004 for the territorial waters.
The first path is quiet: the treaty holds, and the town keeps changing inside its old lines.
Longyearbyen shut its coal power plant in October 2023, and research and tourism now carry more of the town.
The second path runs through the sea: as waters warm, scientists report fish such as cod and mackerel shifting north.
If more fleets come, the old argument over who may fish and drill inside the 1977 line could sharpen, perhaps in court.
For now, Norway has not opened the seabed around Svalbard to oil and gas exploration.

shots.vo: The third path is a crisis between Russia and NATO, when the gap between Bear Island and Norway would matter most.
Article 9 would then face its hardest test: a ban on bases, written before aircraft had even flown to the Pole.

map.label: NATO and Russia around a demilitarised archipelago

shots.vo: Both governments say they want calm: Norway's motto is 'High North, low tension', and Russia calls the Arctic a 'territory of dialogue'.

shots.vo: Which path comes may depend less on Svalbard itself than on the powers that sit around it.
Norway can't close Svalbard to people from treaty countries, because that open door is the price it paid for the islands.

map.label: Norwegian since 1920, open to treaty citizens

shots.vo: The door is not a loophole; it is the deal that made the islands Norwegian in the first place.
